name: Elena Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the haul truck line at Alder Quarry mine and drive the steep route when a new operator needs a guide. I have a two-year technical diploma and know where rain washes gravel across the bend. I use AI daily to sort fault reports before briefing drivers, but I check the original entries. My partner and I have grown children, and care costs for his father left us with less than a month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the drivers that a shorter fault report is useful if we still inspect the trucks. I already use AI to group the reports each day. The road and brake checks still belong to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am well regarded at Alder Quarry, but the pay here is low for a lead operator and our savings are almost gone. A cancelled week would hurt, even if AI mostly stalls. There are very few nearby mines where I could replace the wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep driving and running the briefing. I would test a new AI brake-report feature against the paper maintenance cards for four weeks before using it. I would set aside the pay from any extra shift for the next care bill, if extra shifts came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household, though not about the technology in this picture. The account gets thin before the next payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a wrong report do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A missing brake repair could send a heavy truck down the wet bend. I would stop that truck until maintenance checked the card. A polished fault summary cannot hold a loaded truck on a hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the care bill still coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, my partner’s father needs regular help at home. We share the costs with family, but our part still comes due monthly. I cannot treat an extra shift as certain income.

I would test the **new brake feature** before trusting its summary.
think: My **low pay** and nearly empty savings make a cancelled week hard to absorb.
Few **nearby mines** limit my backup options despite senior skill.
do: **Keep** driving and briefing Alder Quarry haul truck crews.
**Test** the new AI brake-report feature against maintenance cards for four weeks.
feel: **Anxious** about care bills and the thin household account.
S0.quote: A polished fault summary cannot hold a loaded truck on a hill.
fieldNote: She already uses **AI daily**, so the new learning is a brake-report feature tested against cards.
Her senior standing does not remove **income pressure** from lower pay and ongoing family care costs.
She treats extra shifts as **uncertain**, not a fixed savings plan.

steps.text: Keep driving and briefing Alder Quarry haul truck crew
Test new AI brake-report feature against maintenance cards four weeks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say buying and scheduling will change before the truck needs no driver. I would ask the union and mine to let operators test the AI dispatch plan. A planned load is not the same as a safe load on the wet bend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office team may shrink first, but a tighter dispatch schedule could cut my briefing hour or the junior drivers’ breaks. That would lower my pay quickly. My partner’s hours at the repair shop also change, so I cannot count on the second income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the AI dispatch screen with the scheduler during the first fortnight. I would compare its load targets with actual wet-road trips and bring any lost paid briefing time to the union steward. I would keep driving while there were human shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can master another screen, but I cannot make missing pay appear by working faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What evidence would you take to the union?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the roster before and after the AI plan, plus the truck times on rainy days. The steward could ask why the paid briefing was removed. We would have numbers and a safety reason.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to another mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are few within reach. I would call one if Alder Quarry actually cut my hours, but a commute might swallow the extra pay. I would do the sums before applying.

say: I would let **operators test** AI dispatch plans alongside the union.
I would keep the **paid briefing** if the new schedule tried to remove it.
think: A tighter plan could cut **my paid hours** even while haul trucks still have drivers.
My partner’s **uneven repair-shop hours** cannot reliably replace that pay.
do: **Learn** the AI dispatch screen with the scheduler in its first fortnight.
**Compare** rainy-day truck times and take any lost briefing pay to the union steward.
feel: **Anxious** about pay cuts despite confidence with new software.
S1.quote: I can master another screen, but I cannot make missing pay appear by working faster.
fieldNote: She separates **desk scheduling** from hands-on haul driving, but sees an immediate pay route through briefing hours.
Her **AI skill** helps her test targets; it does not protect the household from lost wages.
The union challenge is tied to **rosters and wet-road times**, not a general objection.

steps.text: Learn AI dispatch screen with scheduler during first fortnight

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI by 2028 changes dispatch and records first, while capable robot haul trucks come around 2031. The mine might buy them, so drivers need an agreement before orders are placed. I would ask for paid transition posts and an income bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty in 2028 and sixty-three when capable robot trucks appear. If Alder Quarry replaced our line then, my lower wage would still be the wage paying our care and household bills. We have less than a month saved, and my partner’s repair-shop hours are not steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would pause our planned home repairs this month and bring our bill list to the kitchen table with my partner. I would push the union for a written income bridge and paid safety-testing posts. If the mine posted a paid safety-test job, I would take its funded training while I kept earning on the trucks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I would be awake thinking about the care bill and the first missed payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which repair would wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kitchen window leaks in heavy rain, but we could patch it for another season. I would keep that repair money for care and food. I do not like it, but the numbers force the choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a safety-test job involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ride with the robot trial team and mark every place the truck should stop. I know the wet bend well enough to make the test honest. I would want a real paid robot safety-test post, not a volunteer badge.

I would press the **union** for paid transition posts and an income bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years to thinking AI and roughly eight to capable robot trucks is time to build a real safety role. The mine should publish trial dates and paid posts. I would bring a draft plan to the union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-three when dispatch work changes in 2031 and about sixty-six when capable robots arrive in 2034. I might retire then, but our savings are too thin to count on it. A paid test role could carry us while the pension builds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would enrol in funded remote-truck safety training next year if Alder Quarry posted a paid test position and kept my wages during class. I would test an AI hazard map against our wet-road incident log this winter. I would request a pension projection and compare it with monthly care costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but this is a timetable I can work with. I would have time to prove what the road needs before a machine takes the route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the hazard map have to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bend where rain moves gravel across the lane, and the stopping distance of a full truck. I would mark any miss on the original incident log. A coloured map is only useful if it names the dangerous bend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the test post never appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep driving and ask the union to press for one. Another mine is not a reliable fallback here. I would not pay for training that left our care bill unpaid.

I would take a **draft plan** to the union meeting.
think: At about **sixty-six**, retirement may be unaffordable without more wages.
A paid **safety-test role** could bridge work and retirement if a real position exists.
do: **Enrol** in funded remote-truck safety training if a paid post opens and wages continue.
**Test** an AI hazard map against wet-road incident logs this winter.
**Compare** a pension projection with monthly care costs.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to work against a longer timetable.
S3.quote: A coloured map is only useful if it names the dangerous bend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say ten years to thinking AI and about thirteen to capable robot trucks is enough time to agree who tests them and who keeps a wage. I would ask the union to protect younger drivers as well as older ones. A fair plan needs dates and paid places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-eight in 2036 and around seventy-one when capable robots follow in 2039. I hope to retire before that, but our present savings do not prove we can. Care costs could change, and I would need real pension numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the truck line while shifts remain. I would request a pension projection this year, then ask our family to review how we share care costs. I would help the union write a paid training timetable for younger drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about household money, even though the robot date is far off. The uncertainty is in our bills already, not only in future machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you promise your partner a retirement date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not while care costs and the pension figure are uncertain. We would revisit it after the next statement. I would rather give my partner an honest retirement range than a date we cannot afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would younger drivers need from the agreement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid practice with the new equipment and clear chances at real posts. I would bring a junior driver to the union meeting, not speak for everyone alone. The training clock should start before any truck order.

say: I would ask for **paid places** and dates during the long warning before robot trucks.
I would include **younger drivers** in union talks.
think: At about **seventy-one** when robots become capable, I hope to be retired but cannot assume it.
Our **thin savings** and care costs make pension figures essential.
do: **Keep** leading the truck line while paid shifts remain.
**Request** a pension projection and review family care costs this year.
**Help** the union write a paid training timetable with younger drivers.
feel: **Anxious** about household money despite the distant robot date.
S4.quote: I would rather give my partner an honest retirement range than a date we cannot afford.
fieldNote: The **2039 robot date** may follow retirement, but she will not assume retirement is funded.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robot trucks could arrive around 2031 before our care costs ease. A written income bridge and funded safety training tied to paid posts would help. The union should have a seat in every trial.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays for care when a senior worker loses a shift. I know the wet bend at Alder Quarry mine better than any map, but that knowledge does not cover a bill. A safe trial has to include the people who still need wages.

headlineQuote: I know the wet bend at Alder Quarry mine better than any map, but that knowledge does not cover a bill.
portrait: Elena Lopez is a **58-year-old** haul truck lead at Alder Quarry mine, with a technical diploma, grown children and thin savings.
Ongoing family **care costs** and lower pay make missed shifts costly despite her strong driving skill.
She uses **AI daily**, tests new features against maintenance cards and asks the union to challenge unsafe dispatch plans.
Fast robot availability leaves her **alarmed** about wages; longer warning helps only with paid posts and funded training.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because capable robot trucks could arrive around 2031 while care costs still require wages.
whatWouldHelp: A **written income bridge** and funded safety training tied to paid posts would help her plan.
